findings.issue: Source simile is framed 'As when the two winds ... spring up ... even thus troubled were the hearts'; candidate turns it into a free-standing statement ('Two winds blow from Thrace ... they can spring up') and the closing 'in just that way' loses the as-when/so structure the style note requires.
findings.fix: The Trojans kept watch. But Panic, the comrade of blood-stained Rout, had taken a firm hold on the Achaeans, and all their princes were in despair. As when the two winds that blow from Thrace, the north wind and the northwest wind, spring up suddenly and stir the sea to fury, and at once the dark waves lift their heads and scatter seaweed in every direction, so were the hearts of the Achaeans troubled.

findings.fix: “As for him, the hound does not even dare to look me in the face. I will not sit in council with him, and I will have no share in any plan of his. He has wronged and deceived me enough. He will not cheat me a second time. Let him go his own way, since Zeus has taken away his reason. I hate his presents, and I do not care a straw for the man himself. Let him offer ten times what he has offered now, or twenty—no, not even if he gave me everything he owns in the world, now or ever. Let him promise me the wealth of Orchomenus or of Egyptian Thebes, the richest city in the whole world, which has a hundred gates, and through each gate two hundred men can drive out at once with their chariots and horses. Let him offer gifts as many as the sands of the sea or the dust of the plain. Even so he will not move me until I have paid him back in full for the bitter wrong he did me. I will not marry his daughter. She could be as beautiful as Aphrodite and as skilled as Athena, and I would still have none of her. Let some other man take her, one who suits her better and rules a larger kingdom. If the gods bring me safely home, Peleus himself will find me a wife. There are Achaean women in Hellas and Phthia, daughters of kings who rule cities, and I can take whichever of them I like and marry her. Many times, back home in Phthia, I longed to court a wife who would suit me and to enjoy the riches of my old father Peleus. My life is worth more to me than all the wealth of Ilium in the days when it was at peace, before the Achaeans came, or than all the treasure that lies on the stone floor of Apollo’s temple under the cliffs of Pytho. Cattle and sheep can be won by raiding, and a man can buy tripods and horses if he wants them. But once a man’s life has left him, it can be neither bought nor raided back.

findings.issue: Source 'awful Proserpine' is not in the name map (other names keep Butler's spelling); candidate has 'Persephone'. Also 'whom he loved to the wrong of his wife' is clumsy, and the door/wall sequence is reordered: source 'broke through the closed doors ... and climbed the wall of the outer court after passing quickly and unperceived through the men on guard' while candidate attaches the passing of the guards to the doors.
findings.fix: They all stayed silent, shaken by how harshly he had refused them. At last the old knight Phoenix, in his great fear for the ships of the Achaeans, burst into tears and spoke. “Noble Achilles, if you are really set on going home, and your fierce anger will not let you do anything to save the ships from burning, then how can I stay here without you, my son? Your father Peleus sent me with you on the day he sent you from Phthia to Agamemnon, when you were only a boy. You knew nothing yet of war, or of the skills that make men known in council. He sent me to train you in every excellence of speech and action. So, my son, I will not stay here without you—no, not even if heaven itself were to strip the years from me and make me as young as I was when I first left Hellas, the land of fair women. I was running from the anger of my father Amyntor, son of Ormenus. He was furious with me over his concubine, whom he loved, to the wrong of his wife, my mother. My mother begged me without stopping to sleep with the woman myself, so that she would come to hate my father, and in time I gave in. But my father soon found out, and cursed me bitterly, calling the dreadful Erinyes to witness. He prayed that no son of mine would ever sit on his knees—and the gods, Zeus of the world below and awful Proserpine, fulfilled his curse. I made up my mind to kill him, but some god held back my rashness. He made me think of what men’s evil tongues would say, and how I would be branded the murderer of my father. Even so, I could not bear to stay in my father’s house with him so bitter against me. My cousins and kinsmen gathered around me and pressed me hard to stay. They slaughtered many sheep and many oxen, set many fat hogs to roast before the fire, and broached many jars of my father’s wine. For nine whole nights they set a guard over me, taking turns to watch, and they kept a fire burning always, both in the cloister of the outer court and in the inner court at the doors of the room where I lay. But when the darkness of the tenth night came, I broke through the closed doors of my room and climbed the wall of the outer court, after slipping quickly and unseen through the guards and the women servants. Then I fled through Hellas until I came to fertile Phthia, mother of sheep, and to King Peleus. He welcomed me and treated me as a father treats an only son who will inherit all his wealth. He made me rich and put me over many people, setting me on the borders of Phthia, where I ruled as chief over the Dolopians.

findings.fix: “As long as Meleager was in the field, things went badly for the Curetes, and for all their numbers they could not hold their ground under the city walls. But in time Meleager grew angry, as even a wise man sometimes will. He was enraged at his mother Althaea, and so he stayed at home with his wedded wife, fair Cleopatra. She was the daughter of Marpessa daughter of Euenus, and of Ides, the man who was then alive. This Ides took up his bow and faced King Apollo himself for the sake of fair Marpessa. After that, her father and mother named her Alcyone, because her mother had cried out in grief like the halcyon bird when Phoebus Apollo carried her off. So Meleager stayed at home with Cleopatra, feeding the anger he felt over his mother’s curses. His mother was grieving for her brother’s death. She prayed to the gods and beat the earth with her hands, calling on Hades and on awful Proserpine. She was on her knees, and her bosom was wet with tears, as she prayed that they would kill her son. And Erinys, who walks in darkness and knows no pity, heard her from Erebus.
